{"input":{"new":"/// Check if a recipe line already has error handling
fn has_error_handling(recipe: &str) -> bool {
    if recipe.contains("|| exit")
        || recipe.contains("|| return")
        || recipe.contains("set -e")
        || recipe.contains("&&")
    {
        return true;
    }

    // Issue #209 (Bug 3): Accept compound `|| { ...; exit N; }` /
    // `|| { ...; return N; }` error handlers. These are strictly better than
    // bare `|| exit 1` because they let the user emit a diagnostic before
    // exiting (e.g. `curl ... || { echo "✗ failed"; exit 1; }`).
    // Also recognize terminal commands like die/fail in the tail.
    has_compound_error_handler(recipe)
}

/// Returns true if `recipe` contains a `||` followed by a compound block
/// `{ ... }` whose body terminates with `exit`, `return`, `die`, or `fail`.
fn has_compound_error_handler(recipe: &str) -> bool {
    let mut search_from = 0;
    while let Some(idx) = recipe[search_from..].find("||") {
        let after = &recipe[search_from + idx + 2..];
        let trimmed = after.trim_start();
        if trimmed.starts_with('{') {
            // Find the matching closing brace.
            if let Some(close) = find_matching_close_brace(trimmed) {
                let body = &trimmed[1..close];
                if body_ends_in_terminal(body) {
                    return true;
                }
            }
        }
        search_from += idx + 2;
    }
    false
}

fn find_matching_close_brace(s: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    // Assumes s starts with '{'. Tracks single/double quotes to skip braces
    // appearing inside quoted strings.
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    if bytes.is_empty() || bytes[0] != b'{' {
        return None;
    }
    let mut depth = 0i32;
    let mut in_single = false;
    let mut in_double = false;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < bytes.len() {
        let c = bytes[i];
        if c == b'\'' && !in_double {
            in_single = !in_single;
        } else if c == b'"' && !in_single {
            in_double = !in_double;
        } else if !in_single && !in_double {
            if c == b'{' {
                depth += 1;
            } else if c == b'}' {
                depth -= 1;
                if depth == 0 {
                    return Some(i);
                }
            }
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    None

//!
//! **Rule**: Detect unquoted variables in target prerequisites
//!
//! **Why this matters**:
//! Variables in prerequisites should be quoted to handle filenames with spaces.
//! Unquoted variables like `$(FILES)` will break if any filename contains spaces.
//! GNU Make doesn't automatically quote variable expansions, so this must be
//! done explicitly. This is especially important for `$(wildcard)` results.
//!
//! **Auto-fix**: Add quotes around variable references in prerequisites
//!
//! ## Examples
//!
//! ❌ **BAD** (unquoted variable - breaks with spaces):
//! ```makefile
//! app: $(FILES)
//! \t$(CC) $(FILES) -o app
//! ```
//!
//! ✅ **GOOD** (quoted variable - handles spaces):
//! ```makefile
//! app: "$(FILES)"
//! \t$(CC) "$(FILES)" -o app
//! ```

use crate::linter::{Diagnostic, Fix, LintResult, Severity, Span};

/// Check for unquoted variables in prerequisites
pub fn check(source: &str) -> LintResult {
    let mut result = LintResult::new();

    for (line_num, line) in source.lines().enumerate() {
        // Skip comment lines
        if line.trim_start().starts_with('#') {
            continue;
        }

        // Skip non-target lines (must contain ':')
        if !is_target_line(line) {
            continue;
        }

        // Extract prerequisites part (after ':')
        if let Some(prerequisites) = extract_prerequisites(line) {
            // Find all unquoted variables in prerequisites
            let unquoted_vars = find_unquoted_variables(&prerequisites);

            for var in unquoted_vars {
                let span = Span::new(line_num + 1, 1, line_num + 1, line.len());
                let fix_replacement = create_fix(line, &var);

                let diag = Diagnostic::new(
                    "MAKE016",
                    Severity::Warning,
                    format!("Unquoted variable '{}' in prerequisites - may break with spaces in filenames", var),
                    span,
                )
                .with_fix(Fix::new(&fix_replacement));

                result.add(diag);
            }
        }
    }

    result

fn is_target_line(line: &str) -> bool {
    line.contains(':') && !line.starts_with('\t')
}

/// Extract prerequisites part from target line (everything after ':')
fn extract_prerequisites(line: &str) -> Option<String> {
    if let Some(colon_pos) = line.find(':') {
        let prereqs = line[colon_pos + 1..].trim();
        if !prereqs.is_empty() {
            return Some(prereqs.to_string());
        }
    }
    None
}

/// Find all unquoted variables in prerequisites
/// Returns variable references like "$(FILES)" that are not already quoted
fn find_unquoted_variables(prerequisites: &str) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut vars = Vec::new();
    let mut chars = prerequisites.chars().peekable();
    let mut in_quote = false;
    let mut pos = 0;

    while let Some(ch) = chars.next() {
        match ch {
            '"' => in_quote = !in_quote,
            '$' if !in_quote => {
                collect_unquoted_var_at(prerequisites, pos, &mut chars, &mut vars);
            }
            _ => {}
        }
        pos += ch.len_utf8();
    }

    vars
}

/// Check if the current position starts a variable reference and collect it
fn collect_unquoted_var_at(
    source: &str,
    pos: usize,
    chars: &mut std::iter::Peekable<std::str::Chars<'_>>,
    vars: &mut Vec<String>,
) {
    if let Some(&next_ch) = chars.peek() {
        if next_ch == '(' || next_ch == '{' {
            if let Some(var) = extract_variable_ref(&source[pos..]) {
                if !is_automatic_variable(&var) {
                    vars.push(var);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

/// Extract a variable reference starting at position (e.g., "$(FILES)")
fn extract_variable_ref(s: &str) -> Option<String> {
    if !s.starts_with("$(") && !s.starts_with("${") {
        return None;
    }

    let close_char = if s.starts_with("$(") { ')' } else { '}' };
    if let Some(close_pos) = s.find(close_char) {
        return Some(s[..=close_pos].to_string());
    }

    None
}

/// Check if a variable is an automatic variable ($@, $<, $^, $?, $*, $+)
fn is_automatic_variable(var: &str) -> bool {
    let content = var
        .trim_start_matches("$(")
        .trim_start_matches("${")
        .trim_end_matches(')')
        .trim_end_matches('}');

    // Automatic variables are single character
    content.len() == 1
        && matches!(
            content.chars().next(),
            Some('@' | '<' | '^' | '?' | '*' | '+')
        )
}

/// Create a fix by adding quotes around the unquoted variable
fn create_fix(line: &str, unquoted_var: &str) -> String {
    // Replace first occurrence of unquoted variable with quoted version
    line.replacen(unquoted_var, &format!("\"{}\"", unquoted_var), 1)
}

{"input":{"content":"//! DEPYLER-1133: Oracle Loop constraint enforcement in code generation.
//!
//! Canary test for issue #223. Before this fix, `convert_list_method` consulted
//! only `ctx.var_types` when deciding whether to emit a typed push or a
//! DepylerValue-boxed push. The Oracle Loop pre-seeded `var_types` with learned
//! types, but those were wiped by `ctx.var_types.clear()` at the start of every
//! function body, so downstream functions silently fell back to inference and
//! the generator produced `DepylerValue::Int(x)` instead of `Vec<i32>` ops.
//!
//! The fix routes Oracle-learned types through `ctx.type_overrides`, which
//! survives the clear and is consulted FIRST by the list-method helpers.

#![allow(non_snake_case)] // DEPYLER-XXXX naming convention

use depyler_core::DepylerPipeline;
use std::collections::HashMap;

/// Canary: when the Oracle learns a variable is `Vec<i32>`, the generated Rust
/// must use typed push (`Vec<i32>`) and must NOT box the element via
/// `DepylerValue::Int(...)`.
#[test]
fn test_DEPYLER_1133_oracle_list_i32_avoids_depyler_value_boxing() {
    let pipeline = DepylerPipeline::new();

    // Python source: a list-append loop. Without a Python-side type annotation,
    // inference can fall back to DepylerValue for the element type.
    let python = r"
def collect():
    nums = []
    for i in range(3):
        nums.append(i)
    return nums
";

    // Simulate the Oracle Loop having learned `nums: Vec<i32>` from an E0308
    // round-trip — this is the same shape of map produced by the repair flow
    // in depyler-oracle/utol.rs.
    let mut constraints: HashMap<String, String> = HashMap::new();
    constraints.insert("nums".to_string(), "Vec<i32>".to_string());

    let rust = pipeline
        .transpile_with_constraints(python, &constraints)
        .expect("transpilation with constraints must succeed");

    // Hard invariant: with a learned concrete element type, NO DepylerValue
    // boxing may leak into the output for this variable's push site.
    assert!(
        !rust.contains("DepylerValue::Int"),
        "Oracle learned Vec<i32> but codegen still emitted DepylerValue::Int wrapping.\n\
         This is the DEPYLER-1133 regression. Generated Rust:\n{rust}"
    );

    // And we must see a real push call — not e.g. a fully-inlined no-op.
    assert!(
        rust.contains(".push("),
        "Expected list.append() to lower to .push(); got:\n{rust}"
    );
}

/// Companion: the same Python WITHOUT Oracle constraints may still go through
/// the DepylerValue path (that's existing behaviour we are NOT regressing).
/// This test pins the contrast so future changes can't accidentally make the
/// constrained and unconstrained paths identical for the wrong reason.
#[test]
fn test_DEPYLER_1133_constraint_changes_codegen_output() {
    let pipeline = DepylerPipeline::new();
    let python = r"
def collect():
    nums = []
    for i in range(3):
        nums.append(i)
    return nums
";

    let unconstrained = pipeline.transpile(python).expect("unconstrained transpile");

    let mut constraints: HashMap<String, String> = HashMap::new();
    constraints.insert("nums".to_string(), "Vec<i32>".to_string());
    let constrained = pipeline
        .transpile_with_constraints(python, &constraints)
        .expect("constrained transpile");

    // The Oracle constraint must observably change the generated code.
    // (If they're identical, either the constraint did nothing or the
    // unconstrained path was already typed — both are fine in principle,
    // but for this canary we want proof the override is wired up.)
    assert_ne!(
        unconstrained, constrained,
        "Oracle constraints did not change codegen output — \
         override is not being consulted. Unconstrained:\n{unconstrained}\n\nConstrained:\n{constrained}"
    );
}

[![CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/ci-pending-yellow)](.github/workflows/ci.yml)

LeetCode-style implementation of the classic Two Sum problem.

## Overview

Given a slice of integers and a target value, `two_sum` returns the indices of
the two distinct entries whose sum equals the target, or `None` if no such
pair exists.

## Installation

Add this crate as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
two_sum = "0.1"
```

## Usage

```rust
use two_sum::two_sum;

fn main() {
    let nums = [2, 7, 11, 15];
    let target = 9;
    assert_eq!(two_sum(&nums, target), Some((0, 1)));
}
```

## Development

### Build

```bash
cargo build
```

### Test

```bash
cargo test
```

### Quality Gates

This project uses `pmat` and `pmat query` for code analysis and compliance:

```bash
pmat comply check --strict
```

See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for agent-facing guidance.

LeetCode-style implementation of the classic Two Sum problem.

## Overview

Given a slice of integers and a target value, `two_sum` returns the indices of
the two distinct entries whose sum equals the target, or `None` if no such
pair exists.

## Installation

Add this crate as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
two_sum = "0.1"
```

## Usage

```rust
use two_sum::two_sum;

fn main() {
    let nums = [2, 7, 11, 15];
    let target = 9;
    assert_eq!(two_sum(&nums, target), Some((0, 1)));
}
```

## Development

### Build

cargo build
```

### Test

cargo test
```

### Quality Gates

This project uses `pmat` and `pmat query` for code analysis and compliance:

```bash
pmat comply check --strict
```
